questions.q: A chemical change is a change in which
questions.explain: A chemical change forms one or more new substances. The new substances have different properties from the starting substances.
questions.lo: Identify a change that forms new substances as a chemical change

notes.0: This describes a physical change. In a chemical change the atoms are rearranged, so the products are different substances from the starting ones.
notes.1: Being easy to reverse is a sign of a physical change. Chemical changes are usually hard to reverse because the substances themselves have changed.
notes.2: A change of state, such as melting, only changes how the particles are arranged. Think about what happens to the substances themselves in a chemical change.

questions.q: Which is a characteristic of a chemical change?
choices: it is usually not easily reversed
it can be reversed by evaporation
questions.explain: A chemical change forms new substances, so it is usually not easily reversed. For example, the ash and smoke from burnt paper cannot be turned back into paper.
questions.lo: Identify a change that forms new substances as a chemical change

notes.1: A change in shape, like bending a wire, forms no new substance. That is a physical change. Think about what a chemical change produces and whether it can be undone.
notes.2: If no new substance forms, the change is physical. A chemical change is defined by the formation of new substances, which also affects how easily it can be undone.
notes.3: Evaporation can undo a physical change such as dissolving. Think about whether new substances made in a reaction can be turned back so simply.

why.right: Chemical changes are hard to reverse because new substances with different properties have been formed.
wrong: Chemical changes are hard to reverse because the particles have stopped moving completely.
Chemical changes are hard to reverse because the substances have lost some of their atoms.

questions.q: Water freezes into ice. What type of change is this?
questions.explain: Freezing changes water from a liquid to a solid. Ice is still water, so no new substance forms and the change is physical.
questions.lo: Identify a change that forms new substances as a chemical change

notes.0: Freezing is not a mix of both types. It only changes the state of water, so check whether any new substance has been formed at all.
notes.2: Ice looks different from liquid water, but it is still the same substance. A change in appearance or state alone does not mean a new substance has formed.

why.right: Freezing is a physical change because ice and liquid water are the same substance in different states.
wrong: Freezing is a physical change because the water particles shrink and become smaller as they cool.
Freezing is a physical change because water loses its oxygen atoms as it cools down.

questions.q: Table salt dissolves in water. What type of change is this?
questions.explain: When salt dissolves, it spreads out in the water but no new substance forms. The salt can be got back by evaporating the water, so this is a physical change.
questions.lo: Identify a change that forms new substances as a chemical change

notes.0: Salt seems to disappear, but it is still there in the water. It can be recovered by evaporating the water, so ask whether a new substance was really formed.
notes.1: Dissolving does not form any new substance, so it does not count as both types. Think about whether the salt can be recovered unchanged.

why.right: Dissolving salt is a physical change because the salt can be recovered unchanged by evaporating the water.
wrong: Dissolving salt is a physical change because the salt particles are destroyed in the water.
Dissolving salt is a physical change because the salt melts into a liquid in the water.

questions.q: An iron nail rusts. What type of change is this?
questions.explain: Rusting forms rust, a new substance made when iron reacts with oxygen and water. Rust cannot easily be turned back into iron, so this is a chemical change.
questions.lo: Identify a change that forms new substances as a chemical change

notes.0: Rusting is not a mix of both types. Rust is a brown, flaky substance with different properties from iron, so focus on what has been formed.
notes.1: Rust is not iron in a different state or shape. Iron has reacted with oxygen and water, so think about whether a new substance has appeared.

why.right: Rusting is a chemical change because iron reacts with oxygen and water to form a new substance.
wrong: Rusting is a chemical change because the iron slowly melts and changes its state.
Rusting is a chemical change because a layer of dirt sticks to the surface of the iron.

questions.q: Water droplets form under the lid of a pot of hot soup. This is a
questions.explain: Steam from the hot soup cools on the lid and condenses into liquid water. It is still water, so condensation is a physical change.
questions.lo: Identify a change that forms new substances as a chemical change

notes.0: The droplets form by condensation alone and nothing reacts. Decide whether a new substance was formed before choosing a mixed answer.
notes.2: The droplets are water, the same substance as the steam that rose from the soup. A change of state does not form a new substance.

why.right: Condensation is a physical change because water vapour turns into liquid water without forming a new substance.
wrong: Condensation is a physical change because the water droplets seep out through the metal of the lid.
Condensation is a physical change because steam is made of air that turns into water when cooled.

questions.q: In a word equation, the reactants are written on the
questions.explain: In a word equation, the reactants are written on the left-hand side of the arrow and the products on the right-hand side.
questions.lo: Use word equations to represent chemical reactions

notes.0: The right-hand side shows what is made at the end of the reaction. Think about which side shows the starting substances.
notes.1: No substances are written below the arrow in a word equation. The substances go on either side of it, in the order the reaction happens.
notes.2: Above the arrow is where a condition such as heat may be written, not a substance that reacts. Read the equation from start to finish.

questions.q: methane + oxygen --> carbon dioxide + water. Which are the products?
questions.explain: Products are the substances formed, written on the right of the arrow. Here they are carbon dioxide and water.
questions.lo: Use word equations to represent chemical reactions

notes.1: Methane is a starting substance because it is on the left of the arrow. Only one of these two substances is formed in the reaction.
notes.2: Oxygen is on the left of the arrow, so it is used up, not made. Look at which side shows the substances formed.
notes.3: Methane and oxygen are on the left of the arrow. They are the substances that react, not the ones that are formed.

why.right: Carbon dioxide and water are products because they are written on the right of the arrow.
wrong: Carbon dioxide and water are products because they are written first in the word equation.
Carbon dioxide and water are products because they are both gases at room temperature.

questions.q: Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water. Which word equation represents this?
questions.explain: Hydrogen and oxygen are the reactants, so they go on the left of the arrow. Water is formed, so it goes on the right.
questions.lo: Use word equations to represent chemical reactions

notes.0: Water is what is formed, so it should not be on the left as a reactant. Check which substances react together.
notes.2: This shows water breaking down. The question describes two substances joining to make water, so the order is reversed.
notes.3: Hydrogen is a reactant, not a product. Both substances that react together belong on the same side of the arrow.

why.right: Hydrogen and oxygen go on the left because they are the reactants that join to form water.
wrong: Hydrogen and oxygen go on the left because the lighter substances are always written first.
Hydrogen and oxygen go on the left because gases are always written before liquids.

questions.q: Calcium carbonate breaks down on heating. Which word equation is correct?
choices: calcium oxide + carbon dioxide --> calcium carbonate
calcium oxide --> calcium carbonate + carbon dioxide
calcium carbonate --> calcium oxide + carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Calcium carbonate is the reactant that breaks down, so it is on the left. It forms calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, which are on the right.
questions.lo: Use word equations to represent chemical reactions

notes.0: This shows two substances joining to make calcium carbonate. In this reaction, calcium carbonate is the substance being heated, so think about which side it starts on.
notes.1: Breaking down on heating needs only heat, not oxygen. Also, carbon dioxide is missing from the products, so some atoms are unaccounted for.
notes.2: Calcium oxide is formed in this reaction, not heated at the start. Check which substance is heated and breaks down.

why.right: Calcium carbonate is on the left because it is the single reactant that breaks down when heated.
wrong: Calcium carbonate is on the left because it reacts with oxygen in the air when heated.
Calcium carbonate is on the left because the substance with the longest name is written first.

questions.q: Charcoal burns. ? + oxygen --> carbon dioxide. What is the missing reactant?
questions.explain: Charcoal is mostly carbon. Carbon reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide, so carbon is the missing reactant.
questions.lo: Use word equations to represent chemical reactions

notes.0: Hydrogen contains no carbon, so it cannot form carbon dioxide with oxygen. Think about what charcoal is mainly made of.
notes.1: Carbon dioxide is the product of this reaction. It cannot also be the substance that reacts to make itself.
notes.3: Water contains no carbon, so it cannot produce carbon dioxide. Think about where the carbon in the product must come from.

why.right: Carbon is the missing reactant because the carbon atoms in carbon dioxide must come from the charcoal.
wrong: Carbon is the missing reactant because oxygen changes into carbon when it is heated.
Carbon is the missing reactant because carbon dioxide forms whenever any substance burns.

questions.q: During a chemical reaction, atoms are
choices: changed into other types of atoms
questions.explain: In a chemical reaction, atoms are not created, destroyed or changed into other atoms. They are rearranged and joined in new ways to form new substances.
questions.lo: Recognise that atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in a reaction

notes.1: Atoms are not destroyed in a reaction. Every atom in the reactants is still there in the products, just joined differently.
notes.2: No new atoms appear in a reaction. The atoms in the products were all present in the reactants.
notes.3: One type of atom cannot change into another in a chemical reaction. A carbon atom stays a carbon atom, so think about how the atoms are linked instead.

questions.q: In a chemical reaction, the number of each type of atom
questions.explain: Atoms are only rearranged in a reaction. None are created or destroyed, so the number of each type of atom stays the same.
questions.lo: Recognise that atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in a reaction

notes.0: Atoms are not lost or destroyed in a reaction. If a gas escapes, its atoms still exist, just outside the container.
notes.1: Atoms cannot be created in a reaction. The products are made only from the atoms that were in the reactants.
notes.3: Atoms do not disappear when substances react. They are joined together in new ways to make the products.

why.right: The number of each type of atom stays the same because atoms are only rearranged during a reaction.
wrong: The number of each type of atom stays the same because the reaction stops before atoms can change.
The number of each type of atom stays the same because new atoms replace the ones used up.

questions.q: The reactants contain 4 hydrogen atoms. How many hydrogen atoms are in the products?
questions.explain: Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction. The 4 hydrogen atoms in the reactants must all appear in the products.
questions.lo: Recognise that atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in a reaction

notes.0: Doubling the number would mean new hydrogen atoms were created. Atoms are only rearranged in a reaction.
notes.1: The hydrogen atoms do not vanish. They end up in the products, joined to different atoms.
notes.2: Halving the number would mean hydrogen atoms were destroyed. Atoms are only rearranged, so count what was there at the start.

why.right: Hydrogen atoms are the same in number on both sides because atoms are only rearranged in a reaction.
wrong: Hydrogen atoms are the same in number on both sides because hydrogen is a gas that never reacts.
Hydrogen atoms are the same in number on both sides because reactions always form as many substances as react.

questions.q: Reactants contain 1 C, 4 H and 4 O atoms. How many atoms do the products have?
questions.explain: There are 1 + 4 + 4 = 9 atoms in the reactants. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, so the products also have 9 atoms.
questions.lo: Recognise that atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in a reaction

notes.0: This leaves out one type of atom. All the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms end up in the products, so add them all.
notes.2: This counts only the hydrogen and oxygen atoms. The carbon atom is still there in the products, so it must be counted too.
notes.3: Only one type of atom has been counted. The products contain every atom from the reactants, so add up all three types.

why.right: The products contain 9 atoms because all the atoms in the reactants are kept and only rearranged.
wrong: The products contain 9 atoms because new atoms form to replace those that escape as gas.
The products contain 9 atoms because the reactant atoms change into other types of atoms.

questions.q: The products contain 6 oxygen atoms. How many oxygen atoms were in the reactants?
questions.explain: Atoms are not created or destroyed in a reaction. If the products contain 6 oxygen atoms, the reactants must also have contained 6 oxygen atoms.
questions.lo: Recognise that atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in a reaction

notes.1: Doubling would mean half the oxygen atoms were destroyed during the reaction. Atoms are only rearranged, so the count on both sides matches.
notes.2: Halving would mean extra oxygen atoms were created. The products can only contain atoms that were already in the reactants.
notes.3: The oxygen atoms in the products had to come from somewhere. Atoms cannot appear from nothing in a reaction.

why.right: The reactants had 6 oxygen atoms because atoms are rearranged in a reaction, not created or destroyed.
wrong: The reactants had 6 oxygen atoms because oxygen is the only element that is never used up.
The reactants had 6 oxygen atoms because every reaction takes in the same amount of oxygen.

questions.q: Why is mass conserved in a chemical reaction?
choices: no atoms are lost or formed
the atoms change into other atoms
questions.explain: In a reaction, atoms are rearranged but none are lost or formed. The same atoms are present before and after, so the total mass stays the same.
questions.lo: Recognise that mass is conserved during a chemical reaction

notes.1: No new atoms appear in a reaction. If atoms were formed, the mass would increase, so think about why it stays the same.
notes.2: Atoms of one element do not change into another in a chemical reaction. They keep their identity and are only joined differently.
notes.3: Atoms are not destroyed in a reaction. If they were, the mass would drop. Gases that escape still contain the atoms.

why.right: Mass is conserved because the same atoms, with the same masses, are present before and after the reaction.
wrong: Mass is conserved because the products always take up the same volume as the reactants.
Mass is conserved because the gases given off during a reaction have no mass at all.

questions.q: 12 g of carbon burns in 32 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide forms?
questions.explain: Mass is conserved in a reaction. The mass of carbon dioxide formed equals the total mass of the reactants, 12 g + 32 g = 44 g.
questions.lo: Recognise that mass is conserved during a chemical reaction

notes.0: 12 g is only the mass of carbon. The oxygen atoms also end up in the carbon dioxide, so their mass must be included.
notes.1: 20 g is the difference between the two masses. The masses of the reactants combine in the product, so they should not be subtracted.
notes.3: 32 g is only the mass of oxygen. The carbon atoms also end up in the carbon dioxide, so their mass counts too.

why.right: The carbon dioxide has a mass of 44 g because all the carbon and oxygen atoms end up in it.
wrong: The carbon dioxide has a mass of 44 g because burning adds extra mass from the heat given out.
The carbon dioxide has a mass of 44 g because gases always have more mass than solids.

questions.q: 10 g of a solid breaks down into 6 g of P and some Q. What is the mass of Q?
questions.explain: Mass is conserved, so the masses of P and Q add up to 10 g. The mass of Q is 10 g - 6 g = 4 g.
questions.lo: Recognise that mass is conserved during a chemical reaction

notes.0: 6 g is the mass of P, not Q. Together the two products must have the same mass as the solid that broke down.
notes.1: 16 g adds the masses, which would mean mass was created. The two products share the original 10 g between them.
notes.2: 10 g is the mass of the solid before it broke down. That mass is now shared between P and Q.

why.right: Q has a mass of 4 g because P and Q together must equal the 10 g of solid.
wrong: Q has a mass of 4 g because some of the mass is destroyed when the solid is heated.
Q has a mass of 4 g because heating always removes 6 g of mass from a solid.

questions.q: 50 g of reactants react completely. What is the total mass of the products?
questions.explain: Mass is conserved in a chemical reaction. When 50 g of reactants react completely, the total mass of the products is also 50 g.
questions.lo: Recognise that mass is conserved during a chemical reaction

notes.0: Atoms are not created in a reaction, so the products cannot gain mass. Think about what happens to the atoms in the reactants.
notes.2: Atoms are not destroyed in a reaction. Even if a gas forms, it still has mass and counts as part of the products.
notes.3: The reactants do not vanish. Their atoms are rearranged into the products, which still have mass.

why.right: The products have a mass of 50 g because no atoms are gained or lost during the reaction.
wrong: The products have a mass of 50 g because each product has the same mass as each reactant.
The products have a mass of 50 g because the reaction does not change any of the substances.

questions.q: 18 g of X reacts with Y to form 30 g of products. What is the mass of Y?
questions.explain: Mass is conserved, so the mass of X plus the mass of Y equals 30 g. The mass of Y is 30 g - 18 g = 12 g.
questions.lo: Recognise that mass is conserved during a chemical reaction

notes.1: 30 g is the total mass of the products. That total includes the mass of X, so it is not the mass of Y alone.
notes.2: Adding 18 g and 30 g counts the mass of X twice. The products already include the atoms from X.
notes.3: 18 g is the mass of X. The two reactants together must have the same mass as the products.

why.right: Y has a mass of 12 g because the masses of X and Y together equal the mass of the products.
wrong: Y has a mass of 12 g because the reactants always have less mass than the products.
Y has a mass of 12 g because the second reactant is always lighter than the first one.

questions.q: process by which a substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances upon heating
questions.explain: Thermal decomposition is the breakdown of a substance into two or more simpler substances by heating. The word thermal refers to heat.
questions.lo: Classify reactions as combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation or neutralisation

notes.0: Oxidation is when a substance gains oxygen. The description is about one substance breaking down when heated, not joining with oxygen.
notes.2: Combustion is burning in oxygen, giving out heat and light. Here the substance breaks apart on heating without needing oxygen.
notes.3: Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and an alkali. The description involves only one substance being heated.

questions.q: When a substance gains oxygen, it undergoes
questions.explain: Oxidation is a reaction in which a substance gains oxygen. Rusting and respiration are examples.
questions.lo: Classify reactions as combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation or neutralisation

notes.0: Thermal decomposition is a substance breaking down on heating. It does not involve gaining oxygen.
notes.1: Electroplating uses an electric current to coat an object with a metal. It is not defined by gaining oxygen.
notes.2: Neutralisation is a reaction between an acid and an alkali that forms a salt and water. Think of the reaction named after the substance being gained.

questions.q: A substance heated in oxygen gives out heat and light. This reaction is
questions.explain: Combustion is the burning of a substance in oxygen. It gives out heat and light.
questions.lo: Classify reactions as combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation or neutralisation

notes.0: Photosynthesis takes in light energy to make glucose. The reaction described gives out heat and light instead.
notes.1: Thermal decomposition takes in heat to break a substance down. It does not give out heat and light.
notes.3: Neutralisation is a reaction between an acid and an alkali. The clue here is a substance reacting with oxygen and giving out heat and light.

questions.q: Charcoal burns in a barbecue pit. What type of chemical change is this?
questions.explain: Charcoal burns by reacting with oxygen in the air, giving out heat and light. Burning in oxygen is combustion.
questions.lo: Classify reactions as combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation or neutralisation

notes.0: Charcoal does not just break down on heating. It reacts with oxygen in the air, so think about which reaction involves burning.
notes.2: Neutralisation needs an acid and an alkali. Burning charcoal involves a fuel and oxygen.
notes.3: Photosynthesis happens in plants and takes in light energy. Burning charcoal gives out heat and light.

why.right: Burning charcoal is combustion because the carbon reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and light.
wrong: Burning charcoal is combustion because the charcoal breaks down into simpler substances when heated.
Burning charcoal is combustion because the charcoal takes in heat and light from the fire.

questions.q: Hydrochloric acid is mixed with sodium hydroxide. What type of chemical change is this?
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid is an acid and sodium hydroxide is an alkali. An acid reacting with an alkali to form a salt and water is neutralisation.
questions.lo: Classify reactions as combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation or neutralisation

notes.0: Nothing is being heated and broken down here. Two solutions are mixed, so think about what kinds of substance they are.
notes.1: No burning takes place and no oxygen is needed. Look at whether each substance is an acid or an alkali.
notes.2: Neither substance gains oxygen in this reaction. Identify which of the two is an acid and which is an alkali.

why.right: Mixing hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide is neutralisation because an acid reacts with an alkali to form salt and water.
wrong: Mixing hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide is neutralisation because the acid breaks down into simpler substances.
Mixing hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide is neutralisation because both solutions react with oxygen in the air.

questions.q: glucose + oxygen --> carbon dioxide + water. This type of chemical change is
questions.explain: Glucose gains oxygen and forms carbon dioxide and water. A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen is oxidation. This happens in respiration.
questions.lo: Classify reactions as combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation or neutralisation

notes.1: Thermal decomposition breaks one substance into simpler ones on heating. Here glucose reacts with a second substance, oxygen.
notes.2: Neutralisation needs an acid and an alkali. Look at which substance glucose is reacting with.
notes.3: Photosynthesis is the reverse reaction. It makes glucose and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water, but here glucose is used up, not made.

why.right: This reaction of glucose is oxidation because glucose gains oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.
wrong: This reaction of glucose is oxidation because glucose breaks down on heating without any oxygen.
This reaction of glucose is oxidation because glucose is made from carbon dioxide and water.

questions.q: Rusting occurs when iron reacts with
questions.explain: Iron rusts only when both oxygen and water are present. Iron kept in dry air, or in water with no dissolved air, does not rust.
questions.lo: Classify reactions as combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation or neutralisation

notes.0: Iron in boiled water with no air does not rust. Water alone is not enough, so think about what else from the air is needed.
notes.1: Carbon dioxide is not needed for rusting. Think about which gas in the air iron gains when it forms rust.
notes.3: Iron in dry air does not rust. Oxygen alone is not enough, so think about what else must be present.

questions.q: Which is a property of acids?
questions.explain: Acids turn blue litmus paper red. They also taste sour.
questions.lo: State the properties of acids and alkalis

notes.0: A bitter taste is a property of alkalis. Acids have a different taste and a different effect on litmus.
notes.2: Turning red litmus blue is a property of alkalis. Acids change the colour of litmus the other way.
notes.3: A soapy feel is a property of alkalis. Think about how an acid changes the colour of litmus paper.

questions.q: How do acids taste?
questions.explain: Acids taste sour. Lemon juice and vinegar taste sour because they contain acids.
questions.lo: State the properties of acids and alkalis

notes.0: Soapy describes how alkalis feel, not how acids taste. Think about how lemon juice or vinegar tastes.
notes.1: A bitter taste is a property of alkalis. Acids such as lemon juice taste different.
notes.3: Salty is the taste of salts such as sodium chloride. Think about the taste of lemon juice or vinegar.

questions.q: Which is a property of alkalis?
choices: reacts with metals to give hydrogen
questions.explain: Alkalis feel soapy. They also taste bitter and turn red litmus blue.
questions.lo: State the properties of acids and alkalis

notes.1: A sour taste is a property of acids. Alkalis have a bitter taste.
notes.2: Reacting with metals to give hydrogen is a property of acids. Think about how an alkali feels on the skin.
notes.3: Turning blue litmus red is a property of acids. Alkalis have the opposite effect on litmus.

questions.q: Which substance is an acid?
questions.explain: Citric acid, found in citrus fruits such as lemons, is an acid.
questions.lo: State the properties of acids and alkalis

notes.0: Baking soda is weakly alkaline. It is used to neutralise acids, so it is not an acid itself.
notes.1: Ammonia solution is an alkali. It turns red litmus blue.
notes.2: Sodium hydroxide is an alkali. It reacts with acids in neutralisation.

questions.q: Which substance is an alkali?
questions.explain: Calcium hydroxide is an alkali. It is used to neutralise acidic soil.
questions.lo: State the properties of acids and alkalis

notes.0: Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. As its name shows, it is an acid, not an alkali.
notes.1: Acetic acid is the acid in vinegar. It turns blue litmus red, which is what an acid does.
notes.3: Sulfuric acid is a strong acid. Alkalis are the substances that neutralise acids like this one.

questions.q: A liquid tastes bitter and feels soapy. It is most likely
questions.explain: A bitter taste and a soapy feel are properties of alkalis.
questions.lo: State the properties of acids and alkalis

notes.0: Pure water is neutral and does not taste bitter or feel soapy. These two properties are signs of a particular type of solution.
notes.1: A salt is formed when an acid and an alkali neutralise each other. A bitter taste and soapy feel point to something else.
notes.2: Acids taste sour and do not feel soapy. A bitter taste and soapy feel belong to the type of substance that neutralises acids.

why.right: The liquid is most likely an alkali because alkalis taste bitter and feel soapy.
wrong: The liquid is most likely an alkali because alkalis taste sour and turn blue litmus red.
The liquid is most likely an alkali because alkalis contain soap dissolved in water.

questions.q: acid + alkali -->
questions.explain: An acid reacts with an alkali to form a salt and water. This reaction is neutralisation.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.1: Oxygen is not produced in neutralisation. Think about the common liquid that forms along with the salt.
notes.2: Carbon dioxide is given off when an acid reacts with a carbonate, not with an alkali.
notes.3: Hydrogen gas is given off when an acid reacts with a metal. An acid reacting with an alkali forms a different product.

questions.q: acid + metal -->
questions.explain: An acid reacts with a reactive metal to form a salt and hydrogen gas. The hydrogen can be seen as bubbles.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.0: A salt and water form when an acid reacts with an alkali. A metal reacting with an acid gives off a gas instead of water.
notes.2: Oxygen is not given off when acids react with metals. The gas produced burns with a pop.
notes.3: Carbon dioxide forms when an acid reacts with a carbonate. A metal contains no carbon, so a different gas is given off.

questions.q: acid + carbonate -->
questions.explain: An acid reacts with a carbonate to form a salt, carbon dioxide and water.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.1: Carbon dioxide is given off, but this leaves out one product. An acid and a carbonate form three products in total.
notes.2: A salt and water alone form when an acid reacts with an alkali. A carbonate also gives off a gas that turns limewater chalky.
notes.3: Hydrogen is given off when an acid reacts with a metal. A carbonate gives off a different gas, which turns limewater chalky.

questions.q: hydrochloric acid + magnesium -->
questions.explain: Magnesium is a metal. An acid and a metal form a salt and hydrogen, so hydrochloric acid and magnesium form magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.0: Carbon dioxide forms only when an acid reacts with a carbonate. Magnesium is a metal and contains no carbon.
notes.2: A salt and water form when an acid reacts with an alkali. Magnesium is a metal, so the products are different.
notes.3: Hydrochloric acid forms chloride salts, not hydroxides. Check the name of the salt as well as the gas.

why.right: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen form because an acid reacting with a metal gives a salt and hydrogen.
wrong: Magnesium chloride and hydrogen form because the magnesium breaks down to release hydrogen gas.
Magnesium chloride and hydrogen form because the acid reacts with oxygen dissolved in the water.

questions.q: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -->
questions.explain: Sodium hydroxide is an alkali. An acid and an alkali form a salt and water, so the products are sodium chloride and water.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.0: Hydrogen is given off when an acid reacts with a metal. Sodium hydroxide is an alkali, so check what forms with the salt.
notes.1: Carbon dioxide is given off when an acid reacts with a carbonate. Sodium hydroxide contains no carbon.
notes.2: Sodium hydroxide is a reactant, so it is not the salt formed. Hydrochloric acid forms salts called chlorides.

why.right: Sodium chloride and water form because an acid reacting with an alkali gives a salt and water.
wrong: Sodium chloride and water form because the sodium hydroxide breaks down when it is heated.
Sodium chloride and water form because the acid reacts with hydrogen gas from the air.

questions.q: What gas extinguishes a lighted splint with a pop sound?
questions.explain: Hydrogen is tested with a lighted splint. The splint goes out with a pop sound because the hydrogen burns very quickly.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.0: Nitrogen can put out a flame, but it does so quietly. The pop is a sign of a gas that burns very quickly.
notes.1: Carbon dioxide puts out a lighted splint quietly, with no pop. It is tested with limewater.
notes.3: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. It does not burn with a pop.

questions.q: Limewater turns chalky when which gas is bubbled through it?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide turns limewater chalky. This is the test for carbon dioxide.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.0: Hydrogen is tested with a lighted splint, which goes out with a pop. It has no effect on limewater.
notes.1: Nitrogen does not react with limewater. Think about the gas given off when an acid reacts with a carbonate.
notes.3: Oxygen is tested with a glowing splint, which relights. It does not turn limewater chalky.

questions.q: A gas from an acid reaction turns limewater chalky. The acid reacted with
questions.explain: A gas that turns limewater chalky is carbon dioxide. An acid gives off carbon dioxide when it reacts with a carbonate.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.0: Acids do not give off a gas when mixed with water. The chalky limewater shows which gas formed, and so which substance reacted.
notes.1: An acid and an alkali form a salt and water with no gas given off. The chalky limewater shows that a gas was produced.
notes.2: An acid and a metal give off hydrogen, which does not affect limewater. Think about which gas turns limewater chalky.

why.right: The acid reacted with a carbonate because carbonates give off carbon dioxide when they react with acids.
wrong: The acid reacted with a carbonate because carbonates give off hydrogen, which turns limewater chalky.
The acid reacted with a carbonate because carbonates are the only substances that react with acids.

questions.q: Which metal does not react with hydrochloric acid?
questions.explain: Copper is an unreactive metal. It does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid, while zinc, iron and magnesium do.
questions.lo: Investigate the reactions of acids with alkalis, metals and carbonates and test the gases

notes.0: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid, giving off bubbles of hydrogen. Look for a metal that is less reactive.
notes.2: Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid and gives off hydrogen. Look for a metal that is less reactive.
notes.3: Magnesium reacts quickly with hydrochloric acid, fizzing as hydrogen is given off. Look for a metal that is much less reactive.

why.right: Copper does not react with hydrochloric acid because it is a very unreactive metal.
wrong: Copper does not react with hydrochloric acid because it is an alkali that neutralises the acid.
Copper does not react with hydrochloric acid because it is too heavy to dissolve in the acid.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water?
questions.explain: Pure water is neutral. A neutral solution has a pH of 7.
questions.lo: Use the pH scale to describe how acidic or alkaline a solution is

notes.1: pH 1 is strongly acidic. Pure water is neither acidic nor alkaline.
notes.2: pH 14 is strongly alkaline. Pure water is neither acidic nor alkaline.
notes.3: pH 0 is very strongly acidic. Pure water is neither acidic nor alkaline.

questions.q: A solution has pH 3. It is
questions.explain: A pH below 7 means a solution is acidic. pH 3 is below 7, so the solution is acidic.
questions.lo: Use the pH scale to describe how acidic or alkaline a solution is

notes.0: Only pH 7 is neutral. A pH of 3 is some distance from 7, so check which side of 7 it is on.
notes.1: Alkaline solutions have a pH above 7. Check which side of 7 a pH of 3 is on.

why.right: A solution with pH 3 is acidic because its pH is below 7.
wrong: A solution with pH 3 is acidic because its pH is above 7.
A solution with pH 3 is acidic because its pH is close to 0, which is neutral.

questions.q: A solution has pH 11. It is
questions.explain: A pH above 7 means a solution is alkaline. pH 11 is above 7, so the solution is alkaline.
questions.lo: Use the pH scale to describe how acidic or alkaline a solution is

notes.1: Only pH 7 is neutral. A pH of 11 is well away from 7, so check which side of 7 it is on.
notes.2: Acidic solutions have a pH below 7. Check which side of 7 a pH of 11 is on.

why.right: A solution with pH 11 is alkaline because its pH is above 7.
wrong: A solution with pH 11 is alkaline because its pH is below 7.
A solution with pH 11 is alkaline because its pH is close to 14, which is neutral.

questions.q: Which pH is the most acidic?
questions.explain: The lower the pH, the more acidic the solution. pH 1 is the lowest value here, so it is the most acidic.
questions.lo: Use the pH scale to describe how acidic or alkaline a solution is

notes.0: pH 5 is acidic, but only weakly. A lower pH means a more acidic solution.
notes.2: pH 13 is strongly alkaline, not acidic. Acidic solutions have a pH below 7.
notes.3: pH 7 is neutral. Acidic solutions have a pH below 7.

why.right: pH 1 is the most acidic because the lower the pH, the more acidic the solution.
wrong: pH 1 is the most acidic because it is the value closest to the neutral point.
pH 1 is the most acidic because the solution contains only one type of acid.

questions.q: An alkali is added to an acid until neutralisation is complete. The pH
questions.explain: An acid has a pH below 7. As alkali is added, the acid is neutralised and the pH rises until it reaches 7 when neutralisation is complete.
questions.lo: Use the pH scale to describe how acidic or alkaline a solution is

notes.0: pH 14 is strongly alkaline. When neutralisation is complete, the solution is neither acidic nor alkaline.
notes.1: Adding an alkali makes an acid less acidic, so the pH does not fall. pH 0 is very strongly acidic.
notes.2: The pH starts below 7 because the solution is an acid. Think about whether adding an alkali makes the number go up or down.

why.right: The pH rises to 7 because the alkali reacts with the acid until the solution is neutral.
wrong: The pH rises to 7 because the alkali adds more acid until the solution is neutral.
The pH rises to 7 because any water added to a solution brings it to pH 7.

questions.q: Blue litmus paper turns red in a solution. The solution is
questions.explain: Acids turn blue litmus paper red. So a solution that turns blue litmus red is acidic.
questions.lo: Investigate the effect of acidic, alkaline and neutral solutions on indicators

notes.0: Alkaline solutions turn red litmus blue, not blue litmus red. Think about which type of solution makes litmus go red.
notes.2: A neutral solution does not change the colour of litmus paper. Here the paper did change colour.

questions.q: Red litmus paper turns blue in a solution. The solution is
questions.explain: Alkalis turn red litmus paper blue. So a solution that turns red litmus blue is alkaline.
questions.lo: Investigate the effect of acidic, alkaline and neutral solutions on indicators

notes.0: A neutral solution does not change the colour of litmus paper. Here the paper did change colour.
notes.1: Acidic solutions turn blue litmus red. Here the change went the other way.

questions.q: Red and blue litmus paper both stay the same colour. The solution is
questions.explain: A neutral solution does not change the colour of red or blue litmus paper. Acids turn blue litmus red and alkalis turn red litmus blue.
questions.lo: Investigate the effect of acidic, alkaline and neutral solutions on indicators

notes.1: An alkaline solution would turn the red litmus paper blue. Neither paper changed here.
notes.2: An acidic solution would turn the blue litmus paper red. Neither paper changed here.

why.right: Litmus stays the same in a neutral solution because the solution is neither acidic nor alkaline.
wrong: Litmus stays the same in a neutral solution because the solution destroys the dye in litmus.
Litmus stays the same in a neutral solution because the solution is both acidic and alkaline.

questions.q: What colour does Universal Indicator turn at pH 7?
questions.explain: Universal Indicator turns green in a neutral solution, which has a pH of 7.
questions.lo: Investigate the effect of acidic, alkaline and neutral solutions on indicators

notes.0: Red shows a strongly acidic solution, with a low pH. pH 7 is neutral.
notes.1: Yellow shows a weakly acidic solution, with a pH a little below 7. pH 7 is exactly neutral.
notes.2: Purple shows a strongly alkaline solution, with a high pH. pH 7 is neutral.

questions.q: Universal Indicator turns red in a solution. What is its pH?
questions.explain: Universal Indicator turns red in a strongly acidic solution. Of these values, only pH 1 is strongly acidic.
questions.lo: Investigate the effect of acidic, alkaline and neutral solutions on indicators

notes.0: pH 14 is strongly alkaline, which turns Universal Indicator purple. Red shows the opposite end of the scale.
notes.1: pH 10 is alkaline, which turns Universal Indicator blue. Red shows a solution that is acidic.
notes.2: pH 7 is neutral, which turns Universal Indicator green. Red shows a solution that is strongly acidic.

why.right: Universal Indicator turning red shows pH 1 because red means a strongly acidic solution.
wrong: Universal Indicator turning red shows pH 1 because red means a strongly alkaline solution.
Universal Indicator turning red shows pH 1 because red means the solution is neutral.

questions.q: Why can Universal Indicator show approximate pH values?
choices: it is a mixture of indicators
it is made from red cabbage
it is a single pure dye
questions.explain: Universal Indicator is a mixture of several indicators. Each one changes colour at a different pH, so together they give a range of colours across the pH scale.
questions.lo: Investigate the effect of acidic, alkaline and neutral solutions on indicators

notes.1: Universal Indicator does not work by containing an acid. Its range of colours comes from what it is made up of.
notes.2: Red cabbage gives a separate natural indicator. Think about how one indicator could show many different colours at different pH values.
notes.3: A single dye usually changes colour only once, so it shows only two colours. Think about what could give many colour changes.

why.right: Universal Indicator shows many colours because each indicator in it changes colour at a different pH.
wrong: Universal Indicator shows many colours because its single dye fades more as the pH rises.
Universal Indicator shows many colours because it contains an acid that reacts with alkalis.

questions.q: Red cabbage indicator turns red in a solution. The solution is
questions.explain: Red cabbage indicator turns red in acidic solutions. It turns green or yellow in alkaline solutions.
questions.lo: Investigate the effect of acidic, alkaline and neutral solutions on indicators

notes.0: Red cabbage indicator stays purple in a neutral solution. A red colour shows that the solution has caused a change.
notes.1: Red cabbage indicator turns green or yellow in alkaline solutions. A red colour shows the opposite type of solution.

questions.q: Why do antacids relieve stomach discomfort?
choices: they add more acid to the stomach
questions.explain: Antacids contain weak alkalis or carbonates. They neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach, which relieves the discomfort.
questions.lo: Explain uses of neutralisation in daily life

notes.0: Stomach discomfort is often caused by too much acid. Adding more acid would make it worse, so think about what reduces acid.
notes.2: Antacids are not used to kill bacteria. They act on the stomach acid that causes the discomfort.
notes.3: A strongly acidic substance would add to the problem. Antacids are chosen because they react with acid.

why.right: Antacids relieve discomfort because they contain a weak alkali that reacts with acid to form salt and water.
wrong: Antacids relieve discomfort because they contain an acid that cancels out the pain in the stomach.
Antacids relieve discomfort because they dilute the stomach acid by adding more water to it.

questions.q: Why does weakly alkaline toothpaste help prevent tooth decay?
choices: it neutralises acid in the mouth
it adds acid to the mouth
questions.explain: Bacteria in the mouth produce acids that attack tooth enamel. Weakly alkaline toothpaste neutralises these acids.
questions.lo: Explain uses of neutralisation in daily life

notes.0: An acidic mouth is what leads to tooth decay. A weakly alkaline toothpaste has the opposite effect.
notes.1: Toothpaste is not meant to react with the teeth themselves. It acts on the acid in the mouth.
notes.3: An alkaline substance does not add acid. Think about what happens when an alkali meets an acid.

why.right: Alkaline toothpaste prevents decay because it neutralises the acid made by bacteria, which attacks tooth enamel.
wrong: Alkaline toothpaste prevents decay because it adds acid that dissolves the food stuck on teeth.
Alkaline toothpaste prevents decay because it neutralises the alkalis made by bacteria in the mouth.

questions.q: A cake bakes in an oven. What causes this chemical change?
questions.explain: Heat from the oven makes the ingredients react to form new substances. The cake cannot be turned back into batter, so heating has caused a chemical change.
questions.lo: Identify what causes a chemical change: mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electric current

notes.0: Some reactions need oxygen, but the main cause here is the oven. Think about what an oven gives to the cake mixture.
notes.2: An oven heats the food. It does not pass an electric current through the cake mixture.
notes.3: The oven light is not what bakes the cake. Think about what the oven provides to make the ingredients react.

why.right: Baking a cake is caused by heating because heat from the oven makes the ingredients react.
wrong: Baking a cake is caused by heating because the light in the oven makes the ingredients react.
Baking a cake is caused by heating because the cake mixture only melts and changes state.

questions.q: A plant makes glucose in its leaves. What causes this chemical change?
questions.explain: Plants make glucose by photosynthesis. Photosynthesis needs light energy, so light causes this chemical change.
questions.lo: Identify what causes a chemical change: mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electric current

notes.1: Plants do not use an electric current to make food. Think about what the leaves take in from the Sun.
notes.2: Photosynthesis is not driven by heat. The energy leaves need comes from sunlight in a different form.
notes.3: Photosynthesis gives out oxygen rather than using it up. Think about the energy that leaves take in from the Sun.

why.right: Photosynthesis is caused by light because leaves need light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
wrong: Photosynthesis is caused by light because light is a substance that joins with water to form glucose.
Photosynthesis is caused by light because light heats the leaves until the glucose melts out of them.

questions.q: A copper coin slowly turns green. What causes this chemical change?
questions.explain: Copper reacts slowly with oxygen and other substances in the air to form a green coating. This is a slow chemical change caused by contact with air.
questions.lo: Identify what causes a chemical change: mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electric current

notes.0: No electric current passes through a coin left in the air. Think about what surrounds the coin all the time.
notes.1: The coin turns green slowly at ordinary temperatures without being heated. Think about what the coin is in contact with all the time.
notes.2: Coins kept in the dark also turn green. Think about what the coin is in contact with all the time.

why.right: The copper coin turns green because copper slowly reacts with oxygen in the air to form a new substance.
wrong: The copper coin turns green because sunlight slowly changes the colour of the copper atoms.
The copper coin turns green because the copper slowly melts and changes into another state.

questions.q: A silver medal is coated with gold. What causes this chemical change?
questions.explain: Coating a metal object with another metal using an electric current is called electroplating. The electric current causes the chemical change.
questions.lo: Identify what causes a chemical change: mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electric current

notes.1: Reacting with oxygen forms a dull layer such as tarnish, not a layer of gold. A coating of gold is added in a different way.
notes.2: Light does not put a layer of gold onto a medal. Think about the process used to coat one metal with another.
notes.3: Heating a medal does not coat it with gold. Think about the process used to coat one metal with another.

questions.q: carbon dioxide + water --> glucose + oxygen. Which condition is needed?
questions.explain: This word equation shows photosynthesis. Plants need light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
questions.lo: Identify what causes a chemical change: mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electric current

notes.0: No alkali is needed in this reaction. It happens in green leaves, so think about what leaves take in from the Sun.
notes.1: Plants do not use an electric current. This reaction takes place in leaves during the day.
notes.3: This reaction stops in the dark. It needs a form of energy that leaves take in during the day.

questions.q: Which chemical reaction benefits us?
questions.explain: Respiration releases energy from food in our cells. We need this energy to stay alive, so it benefits us.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.0: Rusting weakens the steel in a bridge's cables, which is harmful and costly. Look for a reaction that our bodies rely on.
notes.2: Decay of stored food spoils it, so it is harmful to us. Look for a reaction that happens inside living cells.
notes.3: Forest fires destroy habitats and pollute the air. Look for a reaction that supplies energy to living things.

why.right: Respiration benefits us because it releases energy from food that our cells need to stay alive.
wrong: Respiration benefits us because it removes all the oxygen from the cells in our body.
Respiration benefits us because it makes food from carbon dioxide and water in our cells.

questions.q: How does painting an iron gate prevent rusting?
choices: it adds oxygen to the iron
it keeps out water and oxygen
questions.explain: Paint covers the iron and keeps water and oxygen away from it. Iron cannot rust without both of these.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.0: Adding oxygen would make rusting faster, not slower. Rusting needs oxygen, so think about how paint affects contact with it.
notes.1: Iron is a metal, not an acid, so it cannot be neutralised. Paint works by covering the surface.
notes.2: Paint does not change how hard the iron is. Think about what rusting needs and how a coat of paint affects that.

why.right: Paint prevents rusting because it stops water and oxygen from reaching the surface of the iron.
wrong: Paint prevents rusting because it reacts with the iron and turns it into a different metal.
Paint prevents rusting because it gives out oxygen that makes the iron stronger.

questions.q: Galvanising prevents rusting by coating iron with
questions.explain: Galvanising is coating iron with a layer of zinc. The zinc keeps air and water away and protects the iron from rusting.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.1: Oil also protects iron, but that is greasing, not galvanising. Galvanising uses a layer of another metal.
notes.2: Chromium is used in chrome plating, which is done by electroplating. Galvanising uses a different metal.
notes.3: Painting is a separate way of preventing rust. Galvanising uses a layer of another metal.

questions.q: Why does vacuum packing slow down the decay of food?
choices: it adds oxygen to the package
it reduces the oxygen in the package
questions.explain: Vacuum packing removes most of the air from the package. With less oxygen, the microorganisms that cause decay cannot grow well, so food decays more slowly.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.0: Vacuum packing does not heat the food. It changes what is inside the package around the food.
notes.1: Vacuum packing does not change how acidic the food is. Think about what is removed from the package.
notes.2: A vacuum is a space with very little air. Adding oxygen would speed up decay, not slow it down.

why.right: Vacuum packing slows decay because most microorganisms that cause decay need oxygen to grow.
wrong: Vacuum packing slows decay because the low pressure squeezes all the water out of the food.
Vacuum packing slows decay because the plastic gives out a chemical that kills microorganisms.

questions.q: Which chemical process returns nutrients to the environment?
questions.explain: Decay is the breakdown of dead plants and animals by microorganisms. It releases nutrients back into the soil for plants to use.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.0: Electroplating coats an object with a metal using an electric current. It does not return nutrients to the soil.
notes.1: Rusting is iron reacting with oxygen and water. It does not return nutrients to living things.
notes.3: Neutralisation is a reaction between an acid and an alkali. Think about what happens to dead plants and animals.

why.right: Decay returns nutrients because microorganisms break down dead matter into simple substances that go back to the soil.
wrong: Decay returns nutrients because dead matter changes into oxygen that plants then take in.
Decay returns nutrients because dead matter melts into the soil without any chemical change.

questions.q: Which air pollutant reduces the oxygen taken up by red blood cells?
questions.explain: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells. This reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry around the body.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.0: Carbon dioxide is a normal waste gas from respiration. The harmful gas here is made when fuels burn without enough oxygen.
notes.2: Oxides of nitrogen mainly irritate the lungs and cause acid rain. They do not stop red blood cells from carrying oxygen.
notes.3: Sulfur dioxide mainly irritates the lungs and causes acid rain. Think about the gas made when fuels burn in too little oxygen.

why.right: Carbon monoxide is harmful because it combines with haemoglobin, so less oxygen is carried in the blood.
wrong: Carbon monoxide is harmful because it dissolves in rainwater and makes the blood acidic.
Carbon monoxide is harmful because it destroys red blood cells as soon as it is breathed in.

questions.q: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form
questions.explain: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rainwater to form an acidic solution. Rain made acidic in this way is called acid rain.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.0: Carbon monoxide comes from burning fuels in too little oxygen. It is not formed when sulfur dioxide dissolves in water.
notes.1: Dissolving sulfur dioxide adds a substance to the water, so the water is no longer pure. Think about the pH of the solution formed.
notes.3: Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide used to test for carbon dioxide. It is not formed from sulfur dioxide.

why.right: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain because it forms an acid when it dissolves in rainwater.
wrong: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain because it forms an alkali when it dissolves in rainwater.
Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain because it removes all the oxygen from the rainwater.

questions.q: More carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater. What happens to the seawater?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form a weak acid. More dissolved carbon dioxide makes seawater more acidic, so its pH decreases.
questions.lo: Show awareness of how chemical reactions benefit us and harm health and the environment

notes.1: When a solution becomes more acidic, its pH falls, not rises. Think about what dissolved carbon dioxide forms in water.
notes.2: Dissolved carbon dioxide does not make seawater exactly neutral. Think about what type of solution carbon dioxide forms in water.
notes.3: Carbon dioxide does not form an alkali in water. Think about how it changes the pH of the solution.

why.right: Seawater becomes more acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form a weak acid.
wrong: Seawater becomes more acidic because carbon dioxide takes the salt out of the water.
Seawater becomes more acidic because carbon dioxide warms the water and raises its pH.
